opus-5.5.text:
Training a multimodal foundation model from scratch is a big decision, and I think about it mostly in terms of what you gain versus what you can borrow.

There's a lot of value in starting from models pretrained on internet-scale text and images. They come with a great deal of world knowledge and common sense: what a school bus is, what a construction zone usually looks like, how people tend to behave. That's very hard to reproduce from driving data alone. So in practice it often makes sense to build on those models, at least for the semantic understanding part.

But driving and robotics are fundamentally different from what those models were built for. Our sensors aren't just camera images. We have lidar, radar, and multiple cameras, all synchronized in time and grounded in 3D geometry. The model has to reason about space and motion with real precision, centimeters and milliseconds, not just describe a scene. And it has to work under tight latency and compute limits on the vehicle. An off-the-shelf vision-language model isn't designed for any of that.

So training from scratch makes sense when the core structure of your problem differs from what existing models capture. That might mean your input modalities, your output space (trajectories, occupancy, agent behavior), or the closed-loop way your model's decisions shape what it sees next. In those cases you want representations shaped by your own data from the start.

The practical questions are then fairly concrete. First, do you have enough data, and enough diversity in it? With a large fleet, you have a very rich source of real-world multimodal experience, but the interesting cases are in the long tail, so you have to mine for them. Second, what objectives give you general, reusable representations? Predicting the future, reconstructing sensor data, and modeling other agents tend to yield features that transfer across perception, prediction, and planning. Third, how do you get it on the car? Usually you train a large, capable teacher model offboard and then distill it into something efficient enough to run in real time.

Where I've landed is that it's rarely all-or-nothing. The most promising approach is a hybrid: take the world knowledge from large pretrained models, and combine it with representations trained natively on your own sensor data, which understand 3D structure, physics, and behavior. You also want a strong evaluation setup, including simulation, so you can actually tell whether the foundation model is making the system safer and more capable, not just improving benchmark numbers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses borrowing world knowledge from internet-scale pretrained text and image models, then combining it with representations trained natively on the model’s own sensor data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that we don't really think of it as starting from scratch in the sense of ignoring everything the field has learned. We're starting from a blank set of weights, but we're standing on a decade of insight about transformers, about scaling, about how to do self-supervised learning. What's actually from scratch is the data and the task formulation, and for us at Waymo that's where the interesting part is.

The core question is: what are the modalities, and what is the objective that ties them together? For driving, you have cameras, lidar, radar, maps, and then you have this very rich behavioral signal, which is what every agent in the scene actually did over the next several seconds. That last one is the thing people underestimate. It's a huge, free supervision signal. Nobody had to label it. The world just tells you what happened. So a big part of our thinking has been, how do we make the model predict the future of the scene across all those modalities jointly, rather than train separate perception and prediction stacks and glue them together.

Then there are a few practical things you confront pretty quickly. One is tokenization. Text has a natural discrete vocabulary. Lidar point clouds and camera frames over time do not, so you have to make deliberate choices about how to compress that into something a sequence model can digest without throwing away the millimeter-level stuff that actually matters for safety. We spent a lot of effort there, because a bad tokenizer puts a ceiling on everything downstream.

The second is scale, but scale in the right direction. We have an enormous amount of driving data, far more than we could ever train on. So the question becomes which data. Most driving is boring. The value is concentrated in rare interactions, and you need curation and reweighting strategies so the model doesn't spend all its capacity learning to go straight on the freeway.

And the third is the thing I'd really emphasize, which is that from scratch doesn't mean in isolation. We've found it very useful to bring in knowledge from general-purpose models, language and vision models trained on the open internet, because they carry world knowledge we'd never get from our own sensors. A sign that says "road closed for parade" is not something you learn from lidar. So the design I find most compelling is a foundation model that's native to our sensor modalities but can be fused with or distilled from those broader models, so you get both the precise physical grounding and the semantic understanding of the world.

So to summarize, I'd say: define the right prediction objective, invest heavily in representation and tokenization, be very intentional about data selection, and don't be religious about purity. Use what the broader community has built where it helps.

r001.rationale: The response asks how to bring in knowledge from general-purpose language and vision models trained on the open internet, and describes fusing or distilling that knowledge into a sensor-native foundation model.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, what do you want the model to understand, and what data will give it that understanding? In autonomous driving, for example, you have images, lidar, radar, and information about how the world evolves over time. Those modalities give you complementary observations, but they have very different properties.

So training from scratch is more than choosing an architecture and scaling it up. You need to decide how to represent each modality, how to align them in space and time, and what training objectives will encourage the model to learn useful relationships between them. You also have to balance the data so that the model doesn’t simply learn to rely on whichever input makes the training task easiest.

And then there’s the question of how you measure progress. A lower training loss is useful, but ultimately you want to know whether the model understands motion better, handles unusual situations better, and supports better driving decisions. I would work backward from those capabilities, while building a training setup that lets us learn from large amounts of data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing data and combining driving modalities, but it does not raise how to incorporate existing internet-derived knowledge into a model trained from scratch.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, what do you want the model to understand? In autonomous driving, you need to understand the geometry of the scene, how things are moving, and how the situation might evolve. So you’re bringing together different sensors, but also information over time. It’s not just about understanding a single image.

Training from scratch gives you flexibility in how you represent those inputs and how you train them together. But it also means you have to get the data and the training objectives right. You want the model to learn useful structure from large amounts of driving data, without relying on a human to label everything.

And then there’s the question of how that understanding translates into driving. A model can do well on a prediction task and still miss something that matters for a safe decision. So I would think about this as a connected problem: the data, the architecture, the objectives, and ultimately the evaluation in the driving system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from large amounts of driving data, but it does not raise how to incorporate existing internet-derived knowledge into the model.
